Copper.overview: Copper is used where electrical and thermal transport are important. Pure copper and precipitation-hardened copper alloys serve different strength and conductivity requirements.
Copper.weaknesses: Pure copper has limited hardness for demanding contacts. Greater alloy strength often costs conductivity.

candidates.name: Cu-Cr-Zr alloy with controlled ageing
candidates.change: Select a specified Cu-Cr-Zr grade and qualified precipitation-hardening treatment.
candidates.benefit: Higher strength and hardness than unalloyed copper while retaining useful conductivity.
candidates.tradeoff: Conductivity is sacrificed for strength; an unsuitable temper may miss the intended balance.
candidates.mechanism: Precipitation strengthening supports a better strength/conductivity compromise than leaving all solute in solution.
candidates.conditions: Grade, product form and ageing condition must be fixed before comparison. No alloy percentages or treatment schedule are prescribed.

candidates.name: Precipitation-hardened Cu-Ni-Si
candidates.change: Evaluate a specified nickel-silicon copper alloy for connector service.
candidates.benefit: Strength and elevated-temperature stability may improve.
candidates.tradeoff: Electrical conductivity must be checked against the conductor requirement.
candidates.mechanism: Ageing reduces nickel remaining in solid solution while developing strengthening precipitates.
candidates.conditions: Connector geometry, temper and operating temperature must match the qualification specimens.

Copper.validation: Compare tensile strength, hardness and electrical conductivity on matching product forms and tempers; add thermal cycling for elevated-temperature service.

Glass.overview: Glass performance depends on composition, surface condition and product construction. Annealed, toughened and laminated glass are distinct options for glazing.
Glass.weaknesses: Mechanical or thermal stress can cause breakage. Fragmentation, edge condition and post-breakage behavior matter.

candidates.name: Thermally toughened glass
candidates.change: Use a qualified toughening process on a suitable glass product.
candidates.benefit: Greater resistance to mechanical and thermal stresses than its annealed counterpart.
candidates.tradeoff: Failure can still occur; fragmentation and spontaneous-breakage requirements need checking.
candidates.mechanism: Surface compression makes tensile crack opening more difficult.
candidates.conditions: Final pane size, edgework, glass type and installation matter. Thermal-stress resistance does not establish a fire rating.

candidates.name: Laminated glass with a compatible interlayer
candidates.change: Combine glass plies using a specified polymer interlayer.
candidates.tradeoff: Lamination alone does not imply higher glass strength; interlayer and assembly performance need qualification.
candidates.mechanism: The bonded interlayer retains fragments and provides post-breakage integrity.
candidates.conditions: Select pane and interlayer construction for service temperature and loading; validate the complete assembly.

Glass.validation: Test bending or impact performance, edge quality, thermal stress and post-breakage behavior on the actual assembly. Fire performance needs a separate relevant test.

Aluminium.overview: Aluminium includes many alloys and tempers. Heat-treatable 6061 is a structural option; product form, temper, joining and finish must be specified.
Aluminium.weaknesses: A welded heat-treated product can lose strength near the joint; dissimilar-metal contact can introduce corrosion concerns.

candidates.name: Specified 6061 alloy and temper
candidates.change: Evaluate a qualified heat-treated 6061 product where greater structural strength is needed.
candidates.benefit: A practical structural option with useful corrosion resistance and joining characteristics.
candidates.tradeoff: Welding can reduce strength locally in the T6 condition; dissimilar-metal contact needs assessment.
candidates.mechanism: A controlled temper in a heat-treatable alloy changes the strengthening microstructure.
candidates.conditions: This is a grade substitution, not a recipe for adding arbitrary elements to an unknown aluminium product.

candidates.name: Anodized 6061 surface
candidates.change: Evaluate an anodizing finish on a suitable 6061 product.
candidates.benefit: A finish option where surface requirements matter.
candidates.tradeoff: Cosmetic appearance may favor 6063; bulk strength is not established by the finish.
candidates.mechanism: Anodizing modifies the oxide surface rather than the alloy bulk.
candidates.conditions: Choose finish requirements and inspect the finished product; no coating thickness or performance increase is predicted.

Aluminium.validation: Compare grade/temper-specific tensile properties, including the welded region, and qualify the chosen surface finish in the actual environment.

Iron.overview: Iron is the base element of steels. Pure iron, carbon steels and alloy steels are different materials; adding a steel treatment does not establish the response of pure iron.
Iron.weaknesses: A generic iron record does not specify a hardenable steel. Corrosion protection and mechanical improvement require different choices.

candidates.name: Compatible zinc coating
candidates.change: Evaluate a qualified zinc-coating system for a suitable iron or steel part.
candidates.benefit: Improved corrosion protection in a compatible service environment.
candidates.tradeoff: The coating is consumed during protection and does not establish higher bulk strength.
candidates.mechanism: Zinc provides a barrier and can corrode preferentially to protect exposed steel.
candidates.conditions: Confirm substrate suitability, coating process, geometry and actual exposure; no corrosion rate or lifetime is inferred.

candidates.name: Qualified hardenable steel and tempering route
candidates.change: For strength or wear objectives, select a suitable steel grade before specifying quenching and tempering.
candidates.benefit: A hardness/toughness balance can be tailored in a suitable grade.
candidates.tradeoff: Tempering reduces hardness and tensile strength relative to the quenched state while improving ductility and toughness.
candidates.mechanism: Heat treatment changes the microstructure; the hardening response depends on composition.
candidates.conditions: Do not transfer a hardening cycle to pure iron, unidentified steel, or austenitic stainless steel.

Iron.validation: Establish composition and current microstructure first. Test mechanical properties after processing and corrosion behavior under the intended exposure.

Steel.overview: Steel covers a family of iron-based alloys. Carbon content, alloying, heat treatment and product form determine which strengthening and protection routes are applicable.
Steel.weaknesses: A family name does not specify a baseline strength, corrosion rate or heat-treatment response. No particular steel grade is assumed.

candidates.name: Compatible zinc coating
candidates.change: Evaluate a qualified zinc-coating system for a suitable iron or steel part.
candidates.benefit: Improved corrosion protection in a compatible service environment.
candidates.tradeoff: The coating is consumed during protection and does not establish higher bulk strength.
candidates.mechanism: Zinc provides a barrier and can corrode preferentially to protect exposed steel.
candidates.conditions: Confirm substrate suitability, coating process, geometry and actual exposure; no corrosion rate or lifetime is inferred.

candidates.name: Qualified hardenable steel and tempering route
candidates.change: For strength or wear objectives, select a suitable steel grade before specifying quenching and tempering.
candidates.benefit: A hardness/toughness balance can be tailored in a suitable grade.
candidates.tradeoff: Tempering reduces hardness and tensile strength relative to the quenched state while improving ductility and toughness.
candidates.mechanism: Heat treatment changes the microstructure; the hardening response depends on composition.
candidates.conditions: Do not transfer a hardening cycle to pure iron, unidentified steel, or austenitic stainless steel.

Steel.validation: Identify grade and delivery condition. Check hardness, tensile and impact behavior after processing, plus the actual corrosion environment.

Titanium.overview: Commercially pure titanium and titanium alloys require grade-specific design. Surface wear problems and bulk structural requirements must be evaluated separately.
Titanium.weaknesses: Galling and wear can control sliding-contact performance. Results for Ti-6Al-4V cannot automatically be assigned to commercially pure titanium.

candidates.name: Qualified surface treatment on Ti-6Al-4V
candidates.change: Investigate an oxygen-diffusion treatment for a specified Ti-6Al-4V wear contact.
candidates.benefit: A literature-supported route to investigate galling resistance.
candidates.tradeoff: Surface-treatment results cannot be generalized to every titanium grade or contact.
candidates.mechanism: A modified surface layer changes the contact response; substrate and treatment conditions remain important.
candidates.conditions: The cited study concerns Ti-6Al-4V and high-temperature galling, not all commercially pure titanium applications.

candidates.name: Compatible solid-film lubricant and counterface
candidates.change: Screen a qualified lubricated contact pair when fretting or galling dominates.
candidates.benefit: Potential reduction of damaging adhesive contact under an appropriate test regime.
candidates.tradeoff: Coating durability and transfer to the intended contact remain unverified.
candidates.mechanism: The surface film changes interfacial contact rather than proving greater bulk strength.
candidates.conditions: NASA evidence concerns TiC/Ti-6Al-4V pins and specific coated counterparts. Treat transfer to another titanium system as an engineering hypothesis.

Titanium.validation: Specify grade, counterface, contact stress, temperature and lubricant; perform a representative wear/galling test and inspect surface integrity.
